etymology: A town in the inheritance of the tribe of Asher, named in the roll of its cities; the name is taken to mean “oak of the king” or, in its ending, “the king” — a witness to the kingship of God.
biblical_def: Alammelech was a town in the inheritance of Asher, named among that tribe’s cities: “And Alammelech, and Amad, and Misheal” (Jos 19:26). It is named nowhere else. The name is taken to mean oak of the king, and its ending carries the word melech, king. A town bearing the King’s name, set in the portion of Asher, quietly confesses the great truth that God is King — not king of Israel only, but King of all the earth. “For God is the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7). The nations rage and the peoples imagine a vain thing, but He that sitteth in the heavens laughs; He has set His King upon His holy hill of Zion, and given Him the heathen for His inheritance. To Him belongs the everlasting dominion: “Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever” (1Ti 1:17). The believer, whose citizenship is in a kingdom that cannot be moved, owns Christ as King of kings and Lord of lords, and bows the knee gladly to Him whom the Father has crowned. A little oak-town of Asher, carrying the King’s name upon it, is a standing witness that the LORD reigns, and shall reign for ever and ever, and of His kingdom there shall be no end.

etymology: A town on the coast of the tribe of Asher, near Tyre; also the name of a Levitical town in Naphtali. The name is taken to mean “glowing” or “hot springs,” from a root meaning heat.
biblical_def: Hammon was a town on the coast of Asher, in the region toward Tyre: “And Hebron, and Rehob, and Hammon, and Kanah, even unto great Zidon” (Jos 19:28). The same name marks a Levitical town in Naphtali (1Ch 6:76). The name is taken to mean glowing or hot springs, from a root meaning heat — a fitting name for a place of warm waters or a sun-baked height. Its name may serve the believer as a meditation on holy fervor, for Scripture calls the people of God to a warmth and heat of spirit in His service. “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord” (Rom 12:11). The lukewarm the Lord abhors: “because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth” (Rev 3:16). A tepid religion, all form and no fire, is loathsome to Him who baptizes with the Holy Ghost and with fire, and whose word was as a burning fire shut up in the prophet’s bones. Let the believer’s heart burn within him as he walks with Christ and hears the Scriptures opened; let his love not wax cold amid the iniquity of the times, but glow with zeal for the house and glory of God. Hammon, the glowing town, quietly rebukes the lukewarm and calls the saint to a holy heat of devotion.

etymology: A town on the coast of Asher, near Tyre; also a town of Judah. The name is taken from a root meaning “to lie” or “to deceive,” hence “deceitful” or “a lie” — the very word for a brook that fails in summer drought.
biblical_def: Achzib was a town on the coast of Asher, near Tyre, one of the places whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher failed to drive out (Jos 19:29). A town of the same name lay in the lowland of Judah. The name comes from a root meaning to lie or deceive; and this very word, achzab, was used of a wady or brook that runs with water in the rains but fails and deceives the thirsty traveller in the drought. The prophet Micah plays upon the name: “the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel” (Mic 1:14). And Jeremiah, in his anguish, dares to ask whether God Himself will prove such a failing stream: “wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail?” (Jer 15:18) — the answer being a thunderous No. Herein lies the abiding lesson of Achzib: the world’s comforts and confidences are deceitful brooks, full in the easy season and dry in the day of need. “Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint” (Pro 25:19). But the LORD is no Achzib; He is the fountain of living waters that never fails, faithful that promised, the same yesterday, today, and for ever. The believer forsakes the deceitful streams of the world and drinks of the River that cannot run dry.
webster_summary: A coastal town of Asher whose name means “a lie” or “a failing brook”; a warning that the world’s confidences deceive, while the LORD never fails.

etymology: One of the fenced cities of the tribe of Naphtali, in Galilee near the sea; the name is taken to mean “the sides” or “steep slopes.”
biblical_def: Ziddim was one of the fenced cities of Naphtali, in Galilee near the sea of Chinnereth: “And the fenced cities are Ziddim, Zer, and Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth” (Jos 19:35). The name is taken to mean the sides, or steep slopes, and Naphtali’s fenced cities were the walled strongholds that guarded that exposed northern frontier against the invader. Yet the walls of a fenced city, however high, were never Israel’s true defence. Again and again the northern cities of Naphtali were the first to fall — to Syria, to Assyria — when the people forsook the LORD; and no fortification could save a people whom God had given over for their sin. The abiding lesson of the fenced cities is that the LORD Himself is the only sure wall of His people. “For I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her” (Zec 2:5). A city walled by God needs no other rampart; a city trusting its own stones, though its walls reach to heaven, is naked when He withdraws. Ziddim, a fenced city of the north, preaches that safety is not in ramparts but in the presence of the living God, who is a wall of fire to those that fear Him, and that except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.

etymology: One of the fenced cities of the tribe of Naphtali, on the western shore of the sea of Galilee; the name is taken to mean “shore” or “bank.” Jewish tradition placed it at or near the later Tiberias.
biblical_def: Rakkath was one of the fenced cities of Naphtali, standing on the western shore of the sea of Galilee: “And the fenced cities are Ziddim, Zer, and Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth” (Jos 19:35). The name is taken to mean shore or bank, from its place upon the water’s edge, and Jewish tradition set it at or near the later city of Tiberias. This shore of Galilee, obscure in the days of Joshua, became in the fulness of time the most hallowed lakeside in all the world, for here the Lord Jesus walked, and taught, and called His first disciples from their nets. “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Mat 4:19), He said to the fishermen of these very waters, and they left all and followed Him. On this shore He stilled the storm, fed the multitudes, and after His resurrection made breakfast for His own by the sea. Rakkath, a fenced town of the shore, is a quiet foretoken of the honor God would pour upon despised Galilee, the shore-country where the great Light would dawn. The believer, reading of an obscure shore-city of Naphtali, remembers that the LORD delights to glorify the lowly and the overlooked, and that the same voice which named the fenced cities of old walked the shore of Galilee to call sinners home.

etymology: One of the fenced cities of the tribe of Naphtali, near the sea of Galilee, famed for its hot springs; the name means “hot springs” or “warm baths.” Not to be confounded with Hamath the great city of the north, nor with Hammath the man of the Kenites.
biblical_def: Hammath was one of the fenced cities of Naphtali, near the western shore of the sea of Galilee: “And the fenced cities are Ziddim, Zer, and Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth” (Jos 19:35). The name means hot springs, and the place was famed of old for its warm medicinal waters, which still flow near the site to this day. It is not to be confounded with Hamath, the great city on the far northern border of the land, nor with Hammath the ancestor of the Kenite house of Rechab. The warm and healing waters of Hammath may serve the believer as a picture of the healing that God gives to the wounded soul. When the prophet cried over the hurt of his people, he asked, “Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?” (Jer 8:22). The balm and the physician are found at last in Christ, the great Healer, who bore our sicknesses and by whose stripes we are healed. The hot springs of Hammath, welling up warm and healing from the earth, are a natural emblem of that grace which flows from God to bind up the broken-hearted and to heal the wounds that sin has made. He healeth all the diseases of His people, in soul now and in body at the last.

etymology: One of the fenced cities of the tribe of Naphtali; the name means “earth,” “red ground,” or “tilled land,” from the same root as the name Adam. Not to be confounded with the city Adam on the Jordan.
biblical_def: Adamah was one of the fenced cities of Naphtali, named in the roll of that tribe’s strongholds: “And Adamah, and Ramah, and Hazor” (Jos 19:36). The name means earth, or red ground, or tilled land, from the same root, adamah, that gives us the name of Adam, the man taken from the ground. It is not to be confounded with the city Adam on the Jordan, nor with the cities of the plain. A town whose name is Earth turns the mind to the great truth of man’s origin and frailty: the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and to dust he returns. “For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust” (Psa 103:14). “The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven” (1Co 15:47). Here is both humility and hope: humility, that we are but earth, weak, mortal, and soon returning to the ground; and hope, that the second Adam, the Lord from heaven, has taken our earthy nature, borne it to the grave, and raised it in glory, that they who have borne the image of the earthy shall also bear the image of the heavenly. A fenced city named Earth quietly preaches that man is dust, but that dust redeemed in Christ shall rise incorruptible. Remember thou art dust; but remember also the resurrection of the just.

etymology: One of the fenced cities of the tribe of Naphtali; the name means “tower of God” or “tower of El.”
biblical_def: Migdal-el was one of the fenced cities of Naphtali, named among that tribe’s strongholds: “And Iron, and Migdalel, Horem, and Bethanath, and Bethshemesh” (Jos 19:38). The name means tower of God. Of all the fenced cities of the north, this one carries in its very name the true secret of a stronghold’s safety, for the only tower that cannot fall is God Himself. “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). David, hunted and hard-pressed, made the LORD his tower: “thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy” (Psa 61:3). The believer’s security is not a wall of stone that a mightier engine can throw down, but the living God, into whose name he runs and is safe. A tower of man’s building may be undermined, battered, and burned; the tower of God abides for ever, and the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. Migdal-el, a fenced city of Naphtali bearing the name Tower of God, is a standing witness that the strength of the saints is not in their own defences but in the LORD, who is their rock, their fortress, and their high tower. Happy the soul that has fled from the wrath to come into that strong tower, and dwells safe under the shadow of the Almighty.

etymology: One of the fenced cities of the tribe of Naphtali; the name is taken to mean “devoted” or “consecrated,” from the root that gives the word for a thing wholly given up to God.
biblical_def: Horem was one of the fenced cities of Naphtali, named among that tribe’s strongholds: “And Iron, and Migdalel, Horem, and Bethanath” (Jos 19:38). The name is taken to mean devoted or consecrated, from the same root, cherem, that gives the word for a thing wholly and irrevocably given up to God — the devoted thing, set apart and not to be redeemed. “No devoted thing, that a man shall devote unto the LORD of all that he hath…shall be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing is most holy unto the LORD” (Lev 27:28). A town whose name is Devoted preaches the whole-hearted consecration that God requires of His people. He will not be served by halves; the offering He seeks is the living sacrifice of the whole man. “I beseech you therefore, brethren…that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Rom 12:1). The believer is not his own; he is bought with a price, wholly the Lord’s, devoted and set apart to His service and glory. As the devoted thing might not be taken back, so the soul once given to God is His for ever, and may not lawfully be reclaimed for self or for the world. Horem, the devoted city, calls every saint to a like consecration — to be wholly the Lord’s, holding back nothing, a vessel set apart and most holy unto Him.

etymology: A mountain in the territory of Dan, in Aijalon, where the Amorites persisted in dwelling and were put to tribute but not driven out; the name means “mount of the sun.”
biblical_def: Mount Heres was a height in the territory of Dan, in the region of Aijalon; the name means mount of the sun. It is remembered for a failure: “the Amorites would dwell in mount Heres in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim: yet the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed, so that they became tributaries” (Jdg 1:35). The Amorites of mount Heres were subdued and put to forced labor, but they were not driven out; they remained in the land, a thorn and a snare. “It came to pass, when Israel was strong, that they put the Canaanites to tribute, and did not utterly drive them out” (Jdg 1:28). Herein is a solemn parable of the Christian’s warfare against indwelling sin. It is not enough to subdue a besetting sin, to bring it under tribute and make it serve us in outward decency, while it yet dwells in the land of the heart. Sin left alive, though mastered for a season, will rise again to trouble and ensnare; the Amorite not cast out becomes a scourge. Therefore the believer is charged not merely to restrain but to slay: “if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live” (Rom 8:13); “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth” (Col 3:5). Mount Heres warns that a sin subdued but not mortified is a sin that will yet undo us; the Amorite must be driven out, not merely taxed.

corruption_paragraphs: Mount Heres faces no postmodern redefinition. The failure it records answers the shallow religion that is content to restrain a besetting sin into outward decency, bringing it under tribute while it yet dwells and lives in the heart, sure to rise again.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the mortification of sin. The Amorite of mount Heres, subdued but not driven out, became a snare; and so does a sin merely restrained. The believer is charged not to tax his sin but to slay it: if ye through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. The Amorite must be cast out, not merely put to tribute.
